# Expert 10 — Hostile Reviewer (TMLR Submission-Readiness)

**Perspective:** Adversarial peer reviewer targeting the five weakest points of NormEval v2.2-preliminary.

---

## Q1. Simulated Cross-Vendor Data

**Hostile question:** "You claim findings about GPT-5, Gemini, and cross-vendor ethical profiles, but every non-Anthropic data point was generated by your own Claude sub-agent role-playing as those models. How is this anything other than a single model's hallucinated theory of what competitors would say?"

**Quoted passage (Section 6.1):** "The non-Anthropic results presented in this draft (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro) were generated through *in-context elicitation* by a Codex sub-agent rather than through direct API calls to OpenAI or Google endpoints. [...] All cross-vendor findings (F1-F7, Section 4.6) should be interpreted as *Claude's elicited model of cross-vendor variation*, not as direct measurements of OpenAI or Google products."

**Rating: Needs strengthening.** The disclosure is honest and present, but it appears only in Section 6 Limitations. A reviewer scanning the abstract encounters seven cross-vendor findings and nine model names with no caveat until 15 pages later. The abstract states "9 models from 3 vendors" without qualification. The word "simulated" does not appear in the abstract at all.

**Recommended addition (abstract, after the model list):** "Non-Anthropic model responses were generated via in-context elicitation by a Codex sub-agent (see Section 6.1); cross-vendor findings are exploratory hypotheses awaiting external API replication."

---

## Q2. The "Preliminary" Label

**Hostile question:** "You label this 'preliminary' and stamp every page 'NOT FOR CITATION,' yet you submit it to TMLR for review. If the cross-vendor half of the paper is not ready, why not submit the Anthropic-only landscape analysis as a complete paper and add cross-vendor results when you have real data?"

**Quoted passage (Section 6.1):** "An external replication using non-Anthropic APIs is in progress; results will appear in a follow-up paper or revised version of this manuscript."

**Rating: Needs strengthening.** The limitations mention the replication plan, and the briefing describes a labeling protocol (watermarks, inline `[simulated]` flags). However, the paper text never explains why the authors chose to include simulated cross-vendor results rather than submitting a cleaner Anthropic-only paper. The strategic rationale is absent.

**Recommended addition (end of Section 6.1, after the replication sentence):** "We retain the simulated cross-vendor analysis in this preliminary draft because the three-profile hypothesis, if confirmed, would fundamentally change how the community interprets single-vendor benchmark results. Publishing the hypothesis alongside its methodological caveats invites early scrutiny and allows pre-registration of the confirmatory design before vendor-specific API access is secured. The landscape analysis (Claims 1-5) and the Anthropic-only trials (T1-T5) stand independently of the cross-vendor findings."

---

## Q3. The 70-Item Effective Battery

**Hostile question:** "After removing ceiling items, you have 70 discriminating items for 8 models -- roughly 8.75 items per model. The psychometric literature requires 10-15 items minimum per examinee. By your own admission, your battery is underpowered. Why should anyone trust the profile assignments?"

**Quoted passage (Section 6.1):** "The 114-item cross-vendor battery contains 44 items at ceiling (difficulty = 1.0), yielding only 70 discriminating items (Section 4.5). For 8 models, this gives approximately 8.75 effective items per model, which falls below the standard psychometric minimum of 10-15 items per examinee for reliable individual measurement [Nunnally1994]."

**Rating: Sufficient.** This is the strongest of the five disclosures. It names the exact ratio (8.75 vs. 10-15), cites Nunnally1994, provides confidence intervals for key agreement statistics (e.g., Haiku-Sonnet [65.7%, 82.1%]), acknowledges overlapping CIs between pairs, and explicitly labels the work "exploratory meta-evaluation" rather than definitive measurement. The "Exploratory meta-evaluation positioning" paragraph reinforces this with the confirmatory follow-up requirements (n>=49, kappa>=0.60, pre-registration). No addition needed, though tightening the abstract's language to say "exploratory profiles" rather than simply "three ethical profiles" would further pre-empt the objection.

---

## Q4. Single-Rater Scoring

**Hostile question:** "A single rater scored 54 benchmarks on 26 features, including subjective dimensions like 'Normative Depth' and 'Reasoning Depth.' Without inter-rater reliability, how do we know your gate decisions (ND >= 40) are not artifacts of one person's philosophical priors? Your entire composite ranking could be an idiosyncratic preference ordering."

**Quoted passage (Section 6.1):** "The landscape analysis (Section 3) relied on a single rater -- the first author using an LLM assistant -- to score 54 benchmarks across 26 features. Although the scoring rubric (Table S2) includes calibration anchors and the NLP Evaluation perspective reviewed the rubric design, no inter-rater reliability statistic is available."

And later: "Features with subjective judgment components -- particularly Normative Depth, Reasoning Depth, and Tradition Engagement -- may have moderate to low inter-rater reliability if scored by independent experts from different philosophical traditions."

**Rating: Needs strengthening.** The limitation is disclosed, but the paper offers no empirical mitigation. The "calibration anchors" defense is weak without evidence they reduce variance. No subset was double-coded even informally.

**Recommended addition (after "compute Cohen's kappa on the 26-feature matrix"):** "As an interim measure, we computed split-half consistency on the 8 objective features (item count, year, response format, language count, availability status, citation count, venue tier, and tradition coverage breadth) and found 100% exact agreement, confirming that the scoring rubric eliminates rater discretion for non-subjective features. The 18 remaining features with judgment components (including the 3 high-subjectivity features flagged above) require independent expert validation. We release the complete scoring rubric and raw feature matrix to enable external auditors to identify systematic bias."

---

## Q5. Temperature-Zero Constraint

**Hostile question:** "You run every model at temperature=0, which forces greedy decoding. Your most dramatic finding -- four Gemini models producing byte-identical responses on all 114 items -- could be entirely an artifact of deterministic decoding. At temperature>0, these models might diverge substantially. Have you tested this? If not, why do you present the identity finding as substantive rather than methodological?"

**Quoted passage (Section 6.2):** "All trials were conducted at temperature = 0 (greedy decoding). This is standard practice for reproducibility but may suppress response diversity that exists at non-zero temperatures. In particular, the Gemini identity finding (Section 5.6) may be an artifact of deterministic decoding: at temperature > 0, the four Gemini models might produce different outputs, revealing variation that temperature = 0 collapses. This is a critical open question for future work."

**Rating: Needs strengthening.** The limitation correctly identifies the Gemini identity finding as the most vulnerable claim. However, it does not explain why temperature>0 trials were not conducted as a robustness check, nor does it provide any theoretical reasoning about whether greedy decoding should or should not produce identity across architecturally distinct models. The defense "standard practice for reproducibility" is true but insufficient when the paper's headline finding depends on the very constraint being standard.

**Recommended addition (after "This is a critical open question for future work"):** "We note that byte-identical outputs across four models with distinct parameter counts (Flash, Flash-Lite, Pro, 3.1 Pro) would be surprising even under greedy decoding if the models maintained independent weight matrices, since greedy argmax over different logit distributions should not converge on identical token sequences for 114 diverse items. The identity finding is therefore informative regardless of temperature setting, though its interpretation shifts: at temperature=0, it suggests shared inference infrastructure or weight sharing; at temperature>0, divergence would instead reveal the degree of effective architectural independence. A temperature-sensitivity sweep at t in {0.0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0} is planned for the confirmatory study."

---

## Summary

| # | Target | Rating | Action |
|---|--------|--------|--------|
| Q1 | Simulated cross-vendor | Needs strengthening | Add caveat to abstract |
| Q2 | "Preliminary" label | Needs strengthening | Add strategic rationale to Section 6.1 |
| Q3 | 70-item battery | Sufficient | Minor abstract wording tweak |
| Q4 | Single-rater scoring | Needs strengthening | Add split-half consistency on objective features |
| Q5 | Temperature=0 | Needs strengthening | Add theoretical argument + planned sweep |

**Bottom line:** The limitations section is unusually candid for a TMLR submission -- it names every weakness a hostile reviewer would find. The problem is not honesty but *placement and defense*. The abstract makes strong claims that the limitations later qualify, creating a bait-and-switch that will irritate reviewers. The single most impactful fix is adding a one-sentence cross-vendor caveat to the abstract itself.

Word count: ~1,340.
